branding._logoNote: REB-459. `logoUrl` used to point at assets/rainproof-logo.png. The wordmark is live text now: it can be re-worded from this file, it needs no new export per tenant, and a screen reader has something to announce. The PNG stays in the repo because scripts/og-card.html still renders it into the share card, which is an image and wants an image.
branding._wordmarkNote: REB-459. `wordmarkFont` names a family that the layout stylesheet has declared with @font-face. Absent, the header name renders in the UI font and nothing breaks — the font is an enhancement, not a dependency. `wordmarkWeight` must match the weight the @font-face declares: RBD Outlined ships at usWeightClass 700 with no other cut, so asking for 800 anywhere would get a browser-synthesised bold, which on an already-outlined face thickens the outline into mush.
branding._wordmarkStrokeNote: REB-459, revised REB-478. Judy: make it bolder, it is a thin font. This is the honest way to do that. The face has exactly one cut, so font-weight 800 would get a browser-synthesised bold that thickens an already-outlined letterform until its counters close. A text stroke thickens the outline itself instead. 0.8 was measured as too much at the old 22px — it began filling the bowls of R and P. REB-478 took the wordmark to 30px, and the SAME stroke reads lighter as the letterform grows, so 0.7 at 30px is roughly what 0.5 was at 22px plus the extra weight Judy asked for. Re-measure against the header gradient if the size moves again; this number is tied to it. Turn it off with 0.

welcome.title: Rainproof NYC Flood Map
welcome.subtitle: How to Use
welcome.lead: The Rainproof NYC Flood Map combines personal narrative with publicly available flood data to create a more comprehensive picture of the extent of flood impacts across NYC. The map provides a platform for New Yorkers to share their experiences with heavy rainfall, identify flood risk in their neighborhoods, showcase community-led actions, and generate new ideas for addressing the challenge.
welcome._stepsNote: The director's copy, 19 August, verbatim: four steps, and the layers toggle leads. `action` and `rest` are separate fields rather than markup inside a string, so the action can be bolded — every step reads as something to DO — while config stays plain text that `esc()` escapes. Step one carries no full stop; that is how it was written.
welcome._mediaClaimNote: Step four promises photos, videos, audio and files, and the form does take all four: `ACCEPT` in js/form.js is image/*, video/*, audio/* and application/pdf. `files` is PDF ONLY — if that ever reads as 'any file' to a resident, this line is where to narrow it.

map._styleNote: REB-468. Judy's own Mapbox style ("Rainproof NYC", account j00by). It is a PRIVATE style, which works because the pk token below belongs to the same account and is what every visitor loads it with — if that account rotates the token or deletes the style, the basemap goes with it. Its ground is hsl(60,0%,91%), a light grey, which matters: every stepped ramp on this map runs pale-to-dark for low-to-high and only reads correctly over a LIGHT ground. Checked on this one — all four still get more visible as the value rises. A dark style was tried first and inverted every one of them, so re-measure before swapping the basemap again.
map._boundsNote: Judy, 17 August: the default view cut off Staten Island and the Bronx. `bounds` is what the map actually loads to now (see js/map.js init and focusNeighborhood's reset) — the same five-borough box the address geocoder is clipped to in js/ui.js, so 'default view' and 'where an address can resolve to' are one extent, not two. `center`/`zoom` stay for story.js's flyTo fallback.

layers.label: Predicted Flooding (Today)
layers.caption: Places that flood today, from heavy rain and from coastal storms
layers._captionNote: REB-512, 17 August. It read "Places that flood today when it rains hard", which described only part of the layer. This extent is the DEP Stormwater Flood Map UNIONED with the FEMA coastal floodplain, and the coastal half is 156 of its 164 square kilometres — so rain-only wording named the smaller component. If this map ever decides to show rain flooding ONLY, that is a real option and scripts/build-floodplains.py has a --rain-only flag for it: it measures 10.3 sq km today against 82.9 in 2100. It is not what ships, because rain-plus-coastal is what the layer has always been.
layers._colorNote: REB-469. Fill only, no stroke: map.js paints a geojson layer with fill-color + fill-opacity and never sets fill-outline-color, so there has never been one. The brand blue #2db4d9 at 0.75, which is a deliberately loud current-day layer; the story pin is #154f9f and stays legible on top of it.
layers._labelNote: Judy, 17 August. Was 'Current Flooding', which reads as flooding happening now when it is a model — the Data Dictionary already called these 'modelled exposure areas, not observations' and the panel was the one place contradicting it. 'Predicted' is Amy's own word from her feedback sheet. Measured for the record: this extent is 95% storm surge and 6% stormwater, so it is NOT a rain-only layer and must not be described as one.
layers._opacityNote: Raised from 0.75 on 17 August, with the layer now drawing on top of 2100. Measured over the 91% basemap across 16 combinations: at current 0.85 / 2100 0.90 the three zones a reader has to tell apart sit 3.21:1 (new-by-2100 vs basemap), 1.51:1 (new-by-2100 vs floods-today) and 2.12:1 (floods-today vs basemap). That is the best worst-case of any pairing tried; her previous 0.75 scored 1.45 on the middle one, so this is a small gain and the draw order is what actually did the work. The zones are worth knowing: 157 km2 floods in both, 74 km2 is NEW by 2100, and only 8 km2 floods today but not in 2100.

layers.label: Predicted Flooding (Future)
layers.caption: Places expected to flood by 2100, from heavy rain and from the rising sea together
layers._colorNote: REB-469. A darker teal of the current layer's brand-blue #2db4d9, so the pair reads as one blue at two depths rather than two unrelated hues. Fill only, no stroke. Deliberately NOT the story blue #154f9f: at full strength that matched the raindrop exactly and swallowed any pin standing on it.
layers._labelNote: Paired with the layer above, same qualifier, so the two read as one question answered twice. The 2100 product is NOT the same product at a later date: it adds sea level rise and a DEP flooding category with no present-day equivalent. That belongs in the Data Dictionary, per Judy's call to keep the panel clean.
layers._stackNote: Judy, 17 August: put today's flooding ON TOP of 2100 so the difference between them is visible. `stackUnder` is read by map.js and inserts this layer beneath ov-current. It exists because REORDERING `overlays.layers` CANNOT DO THIS: f2100 has no defaultOn, so it is added on first toggle, always after current, and always ended up covering it whatever order the array was in. Falls back to the story-pin layer if current has not been added, so toggling in either order is safe.

layers.label: Blocks That Flood Again and Again
layers.caption: Census blocks that reported flooding in 4 or 5 of the 5 years since Ida. About one in six New Yorkers lives on one, and together they carry more than 40% of the city's flooding reports.
layers._captionNote: This read '4,079 blocks ... 42%' and was wrong one rebuild later, at 4,082. Same rule as the methodology block: if you are typing a number into config, it belongs in the overlay's meta instead. The exact counts ride in persistent-blocks.geojson under `meta` — blocks, calls, shareOfCalls, population, shareOfPopulation — and the workbook has them to the unit. What survives here are the two ROUNDED proportions, which do not move when a few hundred calls arrive.
layers._colorNote: JUDY: THIS IS THE ONE COLOUR DECISION HERE AND IT SHOULD BE YOURS. REB-419 measured that only three hue bands are free once the four story colours and the four data layers are placed, so this layer deliberately spends NO hue: two steps of neutral slate, carried by value alone. That is also an argument on the merits — this is an analytical finding about where to look, not a fifth hazard category competing with the 311 layers, and a grey reads that way. If you want it to shout, it needs a hue somebody else gives up.
layers._parkedNote: PARKED BY JUDY, 17 August 2026, for a later phase. `panelHidden` takes it out of the layers panel and out of the key; `defaultOn: false` means it never fetches, so the layer is completely inert and costs a visitor nothing. Same mechanism `neighborhoods` already uses. Everything else here is finished and left intact: the file, the meta, the ordinal ramp and the two open notes below. UNPARKING IS THIS ONE KEY. Do not delete the layer or the geojson to park it — rebuilding this file means rerunning the census-block spatial joins, and the colour decision in _colorNote has still never been made.
layers._unitNote: Persistence is ORDINAL — how many of five years a block reported — not a count, so unlike a call-density layer it does not inflate with block area. That is precisely why this one can honestly be drawn on real census blocks while the three 311 heat layers stay on the equal-area grid. Do not 'fix' that inconsistency; it is the whole point.
layers._hoverNote: No hover. `addHitLayer` builds a CIRCLE layer over the source, which is right for the point overlays and wrong for polygons, so a hover block here would silently do nothing. Each feature still carries geoid, years, calls and pop, so wiring a fill hover later needs no rebuild of the file.
layers.keyFoot: Shaded by how many of the five years since Ida the block reported, not by how many reports it holds. Do not compare these two shades to the 311 layers, which are scaled against their own reports.

layers.caption: Water sitting on streets, reported to 311

source._note: REB-414. All three 311 layers read ONE file and differ only in which column they paint. Frozen weekly by scripts/build-persistence.mjs; see meta.built for the date.

steps._note: Reds on the 9-class version, classes 5-9. Judy, 12 August: more red tone. layers._colorNote: REB-469 follow-on, Judy 12 August: the panel swatch is the ramp's BRIGHTEST step — highest chroma — not its darkest. layers.label: Water in Basements
layers.caption: Water coming up into homes and basements, reported to 311

source._note: REB-414. All three 311 layers read ONE file and differ only in which column they paint. Frozen weekly by scripts/build-persistence.mjs; see meta.built for the date.

steps._note: Purples on the 9-class version, classes 4-8. Judy, 12 August, twice: darkest (5-9) first, then back one notch — slightly lighter. Purples is the palest of the three 311 schemes class for class, which is why this layer moved when the other two did not read the same way. Sliding the window is the allowed move; nudging a single step is not, or it stops being a published scheme and nobody can tell which steps were touched.
steps._scaleNote: Judy, 17 August: this layer gets its own top step at 5+, not the 10+ the other three share. Measured on the frozen pull: 3,904 blocks report it, the busiest has 9 calls, and NOT ONE reaches 10. A shared 10+ top would have left the darkest purple permanently undrawn. The breaks below it still line up with the others at 1 and 2, so the pale end is comparable; only the top differs, and it differs because the data does.

layers._colorNote: REB-469 follow-on, Judy 12 August: the panel swatch is the ramp's BRIGHTEST step — highest chroma — not its darkest. Same rule across street flooding, clogged storm drains and FloodNet, and it is the rule that produced her own pick of #ef3b2c for street flooding. The swatch is the only thing naming a layer's colour before you switch it on, and the dark end of a sequential scheme reads as near-black at 14px. Paint is untouched: layer.color is the panel dot plus the stepRamp fallback, and stops[0] always exists on these layers so the fallback never fires. Water in basements needs no change under this rule: on Purples classes 4-8 chroma rises all the way up, so #54278f is both the darkest step and the brightest one. It is the one layer where the two readings agree — do not 'fix' it to a middle step for visual consistency with its neighbours.

layers.label: Sewer Backup
layers.caption: Sewage backing up out of the drains, reported to 311
layers._colorNote: The panel swatch is the ramp's BRIGHTEST step by chroma, not its darkest — the same rule the other three 311 layers and FloodNet follow, because the dark end of a sequential scheme reads as near-black at 14px. Measured across YlOrBr classes 4-8, chroma peaks at #ec7014 (0.847). The DARKEST step #993404 is what cityData.complaints paints as a NUMBER in the half-mile panel, where it needs contrast on white and gets 7.38:1.

source._note: All four 311 layers read ONE file and differ only in which column they paint. `b` is sewer backup, split out of `h` on 17 August.

steps._note: ColorBrewer YlOrBr on the 9-class version, classes 4-8, taken verbatim. Judy asked for yellow, 17 August. Measured against the 91% grey basemap it runs 1.30:1 to 6.02:1, which puts it in the same family as the other three (street 2.36-10.83, drains 1.23-5.52, basements 1.50-8.30) so no layer shouts louder than the rest. Paler windows were rejected: classes 1-5 top out at 1.75:1, which is a wash across 21,684 blocks. Slide the whole window or re-pick the scheme; do not nudge one step.
steps._clashNote: THIS OVERLAPS FLOODNET, KNOWINGLY. FloodNet is YlOrBr classes 3-6 and shares four of these five values, and both layers are circles. Judy, 17 August: 'yellow for sewer, floodnet stays as is, we'll work on it later.' So this is a recorded trade, not an oversight — do not quietly repaint either one.

layers._caveatNote: The largest of the four at 49.2% of all calls, and the least weather-driven: median 22 calls a day whatever the weather, only 39% of calls above that baseline, DEP finds no city sewer issue in 64% of cases. findings/README.md explains why it is counted anyway. Worth reading before quoting this layer alone.

layers.label: FloodNet Sensors
layers.caption: Instruments bolted to street poles that measure how deep water gets. They record depth, not pictures — there are no cameras in this network.

steps._focusScaleNote: 19 August, Judy: the sensors get lost inside the half-mile ring. Multiplies icon-size while a story's radius is open and returns to 1 on clearRadius, so the citywide sizes below are untouched. Read generically by js/map.js, so any shaped layer can carry one.
steps._note: NO STOPS, DELIBERATELY. Judy, 17 August: 'no color scale when layer is selected, the toolbar is helpful enough' — the hover already reports the sensor name, how many times it measured water, when it was installed and its deepest reading, which is more than a five-colour key could say. layerScales() keys off steps.stops?.length, so having no stops is what removes the key; there is no separate hide flag to find. Every sensor draws the same black diamond at the same size.
steps._removedNote: The ramp that was here until 17 August, kept because it encoded two real decisions and somebody will ask. Slate #64748B at 0 was 'no flooding measured yet', deliberately NOT the palest yellow, because absence of a measurement is a different kind of thing from a low measurement and 184 of the sensors carry it. The four measuring steps were YlOrBr classes 2-5. Also gone with it: radiusScale 1.9, which existed only to keep stepped CIRCLES visible at citywide zoom and is meaningless for a fixed-size diamond. Old stops: 0 = #64748B (no flooding measured yet); 1 = #fec44f (measured water once); 2 = #fe9929 (2 to 4 times); 5 = #ec7014 (5 to 9 times); 10 = #cc4c02 (10 or more times)

layers._colorNote: Judy, 17 August: black diamonds. Black because the yellow ramp it used to carry now belongs to Sewer Backup, and two YlOrBr layers on the same map was the clash she parked earlier that day. Black is the one value no other layer on this map uses, and with the diamond shape the sensors are identifiable by form as well as colour, which is what the amber was doing badly.

layers.label: Green Infrastructure (DEP)
layers.caption: Each dot is one thing built to soak up rain. Dark green is finished. Light green is designed or being built. Most are basins under the pavement you cannot see from the street.
layers._designNote: Judy, 14 August: back to one dot per asset. The binned version counted points into ~110m cells so it could be read like the 311 layers, which made it comparable but hid what was actually there. A resident asking what is near me wants the thing, not the density. `bin` is gone and the per-asset hover is restored from ebcb322.
layers._colorNote: Judy, 17 August: match the built geopoints, the dark green is not in use any more. This is the layer's representative colour — the dot beside 'Green Infrastructure (DEP)' in the Map Layers panel. It is NOT what paints the assets: with a `steps` block the circle takes the ramp, so this value only ever names the layer.

source._note: One row per asset, all three status groups. `s` is 0 for built and 1 for designed or under construction, and rides as a number so the colour ramp can read it; the hover maps it back to words. Written weekly by scripts/build-persistence.mjs.

steps._note: Two stops, and this is a CATEGORY not a scale. Judy's own values, 17 August: #0f7f12 is built, #5ee161 is designed or being built. Light means less certain, which is the right direction — a design submission is not a thing on the ground. These replaced #00441b / #74c476 and are no longer ColorBrewer Greens steps; they are hers, so do not 'restore' them to a published ramp.
steps._shapeNote: TRIANGLES WERE TRIED AND REJECTED, 17 August. Judy asked for them so the DEP assets would not be confused with the 311 dots, then reverted: 'I regret making them triangles. It's actually worse when 311 calls are toggled on. I think the dots, the geo points, were much better.' Do not propose them again without a new reason — the differentiation argument has been tested against the real map and lost. Setting `"shape": "triangle"` here plus `"shapePxByZoom"` is the whole re-do if it ever comes back; the renderer is still in map.js, unused, exactly as the diamond mechanism is. Judy's greens from the same afternoon STAY: they are a separate decision she kept.
steps._legendNote: Stops stay ASCENDING because Mapbox `step` requires it; the key is reversed for display only. categorical draws separate rows with round dots instead of a joined strip, so it cannot be read as a scale. countFrom names a key in the overlay's own meta, so the numbers come from the file rather than from config.
steps._colorNote: Judy, 14 August: the light green was too muted. #a1d99b sat at 1.33 contrast on the hsl(60,0%,91%) basemap, which is nearly invisible at a 2.2px dot. #74c476 is the next step up the same Greens ramp: 1.73 on the basemap, 5.37 against the built dark green, and dE 10.7 from the story green #16A97B. Brighter was measured and rejected: #66bd63 reaches 1.90 on the basemap but falls to dE 8.9 from that story colour, under the threshold REB-419 set when it rebuilt the story palette.

sections.h: Five years after Ida | Hurricane Ida: A Pivotal Moment for NYC
sections.p: On September 1st, 2021, the remnants of Hurricane Ida dropped more than three inches of rain on New York City in a single hour, a record at the time. NYC tragically lost 13 lives. The storm revealed that every neighborhood in New York City could flood. To respond, Rebuild by Design launched Rainproof NYC, an initiative to bring New Yorkers together to turn the concrete jungle into a sponge.

sections.h: Introducing the Rainproof NYC Flood Map
sections.p: The Rainproof NYC Flood Map combines personal narrative with publicly available flood data to create a more comprehensive picture of the extent of flood impacts across NYC. The map provides a platform for New Yorkers to share their experiences with heavy rainfall, identify flood risk in their neighborhoods, showcase community-led actions, and generate new ideas for addressing the challenge.

sections.h: Why should I add my story?
sections.p:
New York City’s understanding of where it floods is largely derived from triangulating 311 data with 450 flood sensors; however, we know that not everyone calls 311 and most blocks do not have sensors, leaving many flooding experiences undocumented.

Stories of lived experience fill in the gaps that data misses. Documenting community stories in a publicly accessible map helps create proof that elected officials and city agencies can’t ignore. This map will become a tool to advocate for the infrastructure and resources needed neighborhood-by-neighborhood, and to spotlight the solutions communities are already building.
We want to hear your stories of:

list2.text: You can press the “Share your Story” button or click anywhere on the map to add your flooding experience, action, or idea.

list2.text: Share as much or as little as feels right. Whether it was a puddle in your hallway or a flood in your basement — every experience helps build the bigger picture.

items.h: About Rainproof NYC (led by Rebuild by Design)
items.p:
Rebuild by Design works with communities and local governments to solve environmental and economic challenges. Our work centers people through data, design, community outreach, research, education, and policy to co-create solutions that strengthen infrastructure and protect lives and livelihoods.

Rainproof NYC is Rebuild by Design’s citywide initiative, launched in partnership with One Architecture & Urbanism, to address increasingly heavy rainfall and flash floods. Since the day after Hurricane Ida, we’ve been combining research, global inspiration, and hands-on collaboration to transform NYC into a sponge. The growing Rainproof NYC network brings together community groups, city officials, technical experts, policy advocates, private sector partners, educators, and more to understand and address flooding in NYC.

method.title: How this map works
method.lead: What's on this map, where it comes from, and when we last pulled it.

sections.p: Everything is counted from Sept 1, 2021, the night of Hurricane Ida. Reports are counted by census block — the blocks the Census Bureau and the city both use, bounded by the streets you walk — so one address calling ten times is not ten places that flood. Around an open story we count what is within half a mile, which is roughly a ten minute walk.

sections._pNote: REB-458. The 311-delay sentence moved here from the place card, where it was one of three caveats delivered before the reader had asked anything. It deliberately states no number of days: that figure was measured once at seven and was twelve five days later. The computed date block directly above says where the record stopped, which is the same fact and cannot go stale.
sections.p: 311 records who called, not where it flooded, so a quiet block may be an unreported one. 311 also publishes on a delay, so the newest days are always missing — the dates above are where the record stopped when we last pulled it. Sewer upgrades are not in this data, so nothing built nearby is not nothing done nearby. And counts rise and fall with how much it rained, so a quieter year is not a safer one.

sources.p: NYC 311 Service Requests. Three kinds: water sitting on streets, storm drains blocked so water can't get away, and sewage or water backing up into homes and basements.
FloodNet, a network of ultrasonic depth sensors on street poles run by NYU and CUNY. They record how deep the water gets. There are no cameras in this network.

sources.h: Things built to soak up rain
sources.p: NYC Department of Environmental Protection. Rain gardens, basins under the pavement, planted strips, porous paving, green roofs and underground storage, counting what is built rather than what is planned.
EJNYC. Areas that flood when it rains hard today, and areas expected to flood by 2100 as the sea rises.
The city's NTA 2020 areas. A pin's neighborhood is worked out on your own device, so no location is sent anywhere to name it.

methodPanel._note: REB-453 round two, Judy 19 August: the dictionary was too technical for a resident. This replaces it as what the Methodology button opens. One card per MAP LAYER, in the order the Map Layers panel lists them, saying four things and nothing else: what the layer is, who publishes it, when it was last pulled, what we filtered. Order is COMPUTED from overlays.groups and overlays.layers, not written here, so a layer added to the map cannot go missing from the panel. Dates are read from each overlay's own meta.built at render time and are never typed. Keyed by layer id; the four 311 ids share one `card` value so that group prints once.
methodPanel.title: Where this data comes from
methodPanel.lead: The Rainproof map is built from the layers below, listed in the order they appear in Map Layers. Each entry gives the source, the date it was last pulled, and what was filtered.

current.what: Where flooding is expected today: FEMA's 100-year floodplain and the wider 500-year area, together with the streets DEP's model shows flooding in heavy rain. All of it is drawn as one outline.
current.publisher: NYC Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice, EJNYC report. Source data: FEMA storm surge floodplain (2020) and DEP Stormwater Flood Map (2020).

f2100.what: Where flooding is expected by 2100: storm surge reaching further inland on a higher sea, the land expected to sit below the daily high tide line, and the streets DEP's model shows flooding in heavy rain once sea levels rise. All of it is drawn as one outline.
f2100.publisher: NYC Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice, EJNYC report. Source data: NPCC3 storm surge projection (2100) and DEP Stormwater Flood Map, future scenario (2080 sea levels).

flood_street.name: Flooding reported to 311
flood_street.what: Flooding reports made to 311 since Sept 1, 2021.
flood_street.publisher: NYC Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications, via NYC Open Data.
flood_street._filteredNote: 19 August audit: this said 'counted by 2020 census block', which is the unit the FINDINGS use, not this layer. scripts/rebuild-flood311-from-cache.py rounds each report to 3 decimal places and counts the cells, and it calls those cells `blocks` in its own log, which is where the confusion came from. About 110 metres at this latitude.
flood_street.filtered: Four descriptors included, one per layer: Street Flooding (SJ), Catch Basin Clogged/Flooding (SC), Excessive Water In Basement (WEFB), Sewer Backup (SA). Records without coordinates excluded. Remaining records grouped to a 110-metre grid.

If you find yourself typing a number into this block, it belongs in the overlay's meta instead.

dictionary.linkHint: Dataset ids, filters and windows, precise enough to re-run
dictionary._unrenderedNote: NOTHING RENDERS THIS BLOCK as of 19 August. `method.methodPanel` replaced it as what the Methodology button opens. Kept because it is the only written record of the endpoint, filter and delivery-model answers a replicator needs, and deleting it is a separate deliberate pass. Its wording is kept in step with the live panel so a future reader is never reading two different vocabularies for one dataset.
dictionary.title: Data dictionary
dictionary.lead: Every dataset behind this map, named precisely enough that you can go to the source and reproduce any figure on it.

freshness.h: Two different freshness stories on one page
freshness.p: Three different things, and it is worth knowing which you are looking at. The citywide findings are a FIXED SNAPSHOT, pulled on one stated date and deliberately not refreshed, so a figure quoted from this map still reads true months later. The map layers are frozen files rebuilt once a week by a scheduled job, so the shading can be newer than the findings. And the numbers beside an open story are neither: those are counted live from NYC Open Data the moment you open it. All three are stated with their own date, and a difference between them is the system working rather than a fault.

datasets.name: 311 Service Requests from 2010 to Present
datasets.publisher: NYC Open Data, Department of Information Technology and Telecommunications
datasets.unit: One row is one report to 311. Ten reports about the same corner are ten rows, which is why every figure counts census blocks rather than reports.
datasets.excludes: Rows with no coordinates. Any descriptor other than the four listed. Anything before the window opens.

datasets.name: DEP Green Infrastructure
datasets.publisher: NYC Open Data, Department of Environmental Protection
datasets.unit: One row is one built asset, not one project. The assets on this map belong to roughly 492 projects, so counting them as projects would oversell the number about 28 times over.
datasets.excludes: Anything not built. The filter keeps status_gro='Constructed' only, which drops assets that are designed, in construction or planned.
datasets.note: The layer is named for what it holds rather than for its three biggest families. Every asset type in it is listed below.

datasets.name: FloodNet flood sensors and flood events
datasets.publisher: NYC Open Data, published for FloodNet, a network run by NYU and CUNY
datasets.unit: One row is one sensor, joined to its own recorded flood events. Two datasets, joined at build time, because the useful answer needs both and the portal cannot join them in one request.
datasets.excludes: Nothing is filtered out. Sensors that have never measured flooding are kept and counted, because a quiet sensor is usually a new one and dropping them would make the network look wetter than it is.
datasets.note: 64 tidal sensors are 13% of the network and carry about 70% of every flood event in it. Any total taken from this dataset without saying so is measuring the tide.

datasets.name: Predicted flooding: stormwater and storm surge
datasets.publisher: NYC Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice (EJNYC report), combining DEP's Stormwater Flood Map with FEMA's floodplain for today and the NPCC3 2100 storm surge projection for the future scenario
datasets.unit: One row is one polygon. These are MODELLED areas, not observations, and nothing on this map is counted from them. Two hazards are unioned into each layer: stormwater, meaning rain that cannot drain away, and storm surge, meaning water pushed in from the sea.
datasets.excludes: Nothing is filtered out. But the two years are not the same product: the 2100 stormwater scenario carries a DEP flooding category (future high tides) that has no present-day equivalent, and it is the largest of its three. Today's coastal extent is FEMA's; 2100's is NPCC3's. So the pair shows how much further the water goes, not one dataset at two dates.
datasets.note: Worth knowing before reading either layer: today's extent is 164 square kilometres and 95% of that is storm surge — the stormwater share is 10 square kilometres. By 2100 the extent is 228 square kilometres, and the two hazards move very differently: stormwater grows about eightfold, storm surge about 1.2 times. This map's subject is rain that cannot drain, which is the smaller share today and the faster-growing one. Drawn to give a reader the official picture to compare the reports against — these are the maps this archive exists to test, not evidence in it.
datasets._deliveryNote: Was 'static', described as 'drawn as supplied'. That stopped being true on 17 August: REB-512 found the 2100 layer covered less than half the area of today's, which is backwards, and rebuilt both from the four DEP and NPCC component files by geometric union with 20-metre simplification. scripts/build-floodplains.py is the build and it refuses to write if the future extent is not larger than the present one.

datasets.name: 2020 Neighborhood Tabulation Areas
datasets.unit: One row is one neighborhood boundary. A pin's neighborhood is worked out on the device against this file, so no location is ever sent anywhere to be named.
